# Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Pediatric surgery > Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/mQ0V9f)

---

## Summary

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD) is a <u>self-limited</u>, <u>idiopathic</u> <u>avascular necrosis of the femoral head</u> that typically affects children 4–10 years of age. LCPD is characterized by <u>antalgic gait</u>, restricted <u>range of motion</u> (especially <u>internal rotation</u> and <u>abduction</u>) of the affected hip, and <u>pain</u> in the hip, upper leg, and/or knee. The disease is bilateral in 10–20% of patients. Diagnosis is typically made based on <u>x-ray</u> findings. <u>MRI</u> is indicated if <u>x-ray</u> findings are equivocal and clinical suspicion persists. Management is aimed at preserving the shape of the femoral head and the integrity of the <u>hip joint</u> during healing. Most patients are <u>managed conservatively</u> (e.g., <u>physical therapy</u>, <u>pain management</u>, restriction of <u>weight-bearing</u> activities). <u>Surgery</u> may be indicated in patients > 8 years of age and/or those with more severe disease. Early-onset <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the affected hip is a complication of LCPD.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (4:1) [[1]](/library/czba7w)

* Age: 4–10 years

* <u>Incidence</u> (in children < 15 years): 1–3:20,000 [[2]](/library/Xzb9rw)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u> disease

* Multiple factors might promote the development and progress of the condition, including: [[1]](/library/czba7w)

* Repetitive microtrauma (e.g., due to child's hyperactivity)

* <u>Bleeding disorders</u> (e.g., excess <u>factor VII</u>, <u>factor V Leiden</u>, <u>protein S deficiency</u>)  [[3]](/library/WYXPL9)

* Genetic factors (e.g., possible mutations in COL2A1 <u>gene</u>) [[2]](/library/Xzb9rw)

* Environmental factors (e.g., maternal smoking, <u>secondhand smoke</u> exposure) [[4]](/library/dYXoL9)[[5]](/library/VYXGL9)

---

## Pathophysiology

<u>Avascular necrosis</u> of the femoral head due to a mismatch between the rapid growth of the femoral <u>epiphyses</u> and the slower development of adequate blood supply to the area

---

## Clinical features

* Typically unilateral; 10–20% of patients have bilateral involvement [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)[[7]](/library/xFdE470)

* Gait abnormalities, including: [[8]](/library/bWdHPK0)

* <u>Antalgic gait</u>

* Limping due to, e.g.:

* <u>Limb length discrepancy</u>

* Restricted <u>range of motion</u> (especially <u>internal rotation</u> and <u>abduction</u> of the hip) [[7]](/library/xFdE470)[[9]](/library/iAWJjL0)

* <u>Trendelenburg gait</u>

* <u>Pain</u> in the hip and/or the upper leg, sometimes referred to the knee [[7]](/library/xFdE470)[[9]](/library/iAWJjL0)

* Insidious onset, <u>pain</u> may fluctuate depending on physical activity

* Often exacerbated by <u>internal rotation</u>

* Groin tenderness on palpation

* Hinge abduction  [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)

* Painful and restricted hip <u>abduction</u>

* A sign of advanced disease

* On hip <u>abduction</u>, the deformed <u>lateral</u> pillar of the femoral head impinges on the <u>acetabular</u> rim, preventing the femoral head from entering the <u>acetabulum</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Consider LCPD as a cause of <u>referred pain</u> in a child presenting with <u>knee pain</u>. [[9]](/library/iAWJjL0)

## Diagnosis

<u>Diagnosis of LCPD</u> is typically made based on <u>x-ray</u> findings. <u>MRI</u> is indicated if <u>x-ray</u> findings are equivocal and clinical suspicion persists. [[10]](/library/CFdq470)[[11]](/library/O1WIS40)




### <u>X-ray</u> <u>pelvis</u> and hip [[10]](/library/CFdq470)[[11]](/library/O1WIS40)




* Indication: : initial imaging modality for suspected LCPD

* Views: <u>anterior</u>-<u>posterior</u> view of the <u>pelvis</u> and bilateral <u>frog-leg lateral view</u> of the hip

* Findings [[9]](/library/iAWJjL0)[[10]](/library/CFdq470)

* Frequently normal during early stages of the disease

* Flattening of the femoral head with increased <u>radiodensity</u>   [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)

* <u>Joint</u> space widening  [[12]](/library/9FdN470)

* Subchondral <u>fracture</u> and lucency

* Femoral head fragmentation  [[12]](/library/9FdN470)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>X-ray</u> findings are often normal in the early stages of LCPD. [[10]](/library/CFdq470)

### <u>MRI</u> <u>pelvis</u> without IV contrast [[10]](/library/CFdq470)[[11]](/library/O1WIS40)




* Indication: clinical suspicion for LCPD despite normal or equivocal <u>x-ray</u> findings

* Findings [[13]](/library/cBda-H0)

* <u>Bone marrow</u> <u>edema</u> and epiphyseal abnormalities of the femoral head (early finding)

* <u>Joint effusion</u>

* Other findings are similar to those seen on <u>x-ray</u>





> [!TIP]
> Findings of <u>osteonecrosis</u> are visible on <u>MRI</u> before they become apparent on <u>x-ray</u>. [[10]](/library/CFdq470)[[11]](/library/O1WIS40)

## Management

LCPD is <u>self-limited</u> and typically resolves within 2–5 years. Management aims to preserve the shape of the femoral head and the integrity of the affected <u>hip joint</u> during healing. [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)




### Initial management [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)[[14]](/library/nEd7w70)




* Restrict <u>weight-bearing</u> activities (e.g., sports, dance, jumping).

* Use <u>nonopioid oral analgesia in children</u> (e.g., acetominophen, <u>NSAIDs</u>) to manage <u>pain</u>.

* Refer to a pediatric orthopedic specialist for further management.





### <u>Conservative management</u> [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)[[14]](/library/nEd7w70)




* Most patients are <u>managed conservatively</u>.

* Management may include:

* Individualized <u>physical therapy</u> (e.g., <u>range of motion exercises</u>, stretching, hydrotherapy, supervised <u>weight-bearing</u>)

* <u>Skeletal traction</u>

* <u>Abduction</u> bracing  [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)[[12]](/library/9FdN470)





### <u>Surgery</u> [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)




* Indicated for children > 8 years and/or those with more severe disease, e.g.: 

* Progressive or severe deformity of the femoral head

* Persistent <u>range of motion</u> restriction

* Procedure: <u>pelvic</u> and/or <u>femoral osteotomy</u>





![Surgical treatment of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: intertrochanteric varus osteotomy](media/qldjtkx0uh890qusxezjt42v.jpg)

Surgical treatment of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: intertrochanteric varus osteotomy

## Complications

* Early-onset <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the <u>hip joint</u> due to any of the following: [[1]](/library/czba7w)

* Incongruence between the femoral head and <u>acetabulum</u>

* Shortening of the femoral neck  featuring trochanteric elevation, which can manifest as <u>Trendelenburg sign</u>

* Lateralization and coxa magna (broadening of the femoral head), which can manifest as <u>hinge abduction</u>

* <u>Total hip arthroplasty</u> can be considered in adults that develop <u>osteoarthritis</u>. [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prognosis

Factors associated with a less favorable prognosis include: [[6]](/library/_ud5F70)




* Older age of onset (> 8 years)

* Extensive damage to the femoral head (e.g., <u>lateral pillar classification</u> B/C, C; femoral head subluxation)

* Poor <u>range of motion</u>

* Female sex
